dialogs.title: Dialogue — Einen Termin machen
dialogs.intro: Budi calls a dentist's office. Phone calls in Germany follow a fixed pattern — and they start with your own name, not "hello".

lines.speaker: Praxis:
lines.text: Zahnarztpraxis Dr. Beck, Schneider, guten Morgen.
lines.id: Dr. Beck's dental office, Schneider speaking, good morning.
lines.literal: tooth-doctor-practice Dr. Beck, Schneider, good morning.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Guten Morgen, hier ist Budi Santoso. Ich möchte einen Termin machen.
lines.id: Good morning, this is Budi Santoso. I'd like to make an appointment.
lines.literal: good morning, here is Budi Santoso. I would-like an appointment make.

lines.speaker: Praxis:
lines.id: Of course. Are you in pain?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nein, es ist nur eine Kontrolle.
lines.literal: no, it is only a check.

lines.speaker: Praxis:
lines.text: Gut. Können Sie am Dienstag um zehn Uhr?
lines.id: Good. Can you make Tuesday at ten?
lines.literal: good. can you on Tuesday at ten o'clock?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Am Dienstag habe ich leider Kurs bis zwölf.
lines.id: Unfortunately I have class until twelve on Tuesday.
lines.literal: on Tuesday have I unfortunately course until twelve.

lines.speaker: Praxis:
lines.text: Und am Donnerstag um halb vier?
lines.literal: and on Thursday at half four?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Am Donnerstag passt gut. Der wievielte ist das?
lines.id: Thursday works well. What's the date?
lines.literal: on Thursday fits well. the how-many-th is that?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Also am elften September um fünfzehn Uhr dreißig.
lines.literal: so on-the eleventh September at fifteen o'clock thirty.

lines.speaker: Praxis:
lines.text: Genau. Bringen Sie bitte Ihre Versichertenkarte mit.
lines.id: Exactly. Please bring your health insurance card.
lines.literal: exactly. bring you please your insured-card along.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mache ich. Vielen Dank und auf Wiederhören.
lines.id: Will do. Thank you very much, and goodbye.
lines.literal: do I. many thanks and until hearing-again.

notes: **A German phone call starts with a name, not "hello".** The person answering gives the name of the place and then their own name; the caller says *Hier ist… / Mein Name ist…* Answering the phone with just *Hallo?* sounds like an unknown number.
***Auf Wiederhören*** ends a phone call — "until we hear each other again", since you can't see each other. Using *Auf Wiedersehen* on the phone isn't wrong, but this is the proper form.

***am* for days and dates, *im* for months and seasons, *um* for clock times.** Three short words, three different territories: *am Montag*, *im Mai*, *um acht*. Rather like English *on*, *in* and *at* — and one of the three will turn up in almost every time sentence you make.

**Dates use ordinal numbers, and ordinals end in -e or -en.** *der elfte September* (when naming it), but *am elft**en** September* (after *am*). This small change is hard to avoid, so learn the pair: *der erste / am ersten*.

***Der wievielte ist heute?*** = "what's the date today?". The word *wievielte* ("the how-many-th") is long and awkward, but there's no shorter version — this question comes up in every German office.
***leider*** ("unfortunately") softens a refusal. Turning down a suggested time without *leider* sounds cold: compare *Am Dienstag habe ich Kurs* with *Am Dienstag habe ich **leider** Kurs*.

grammars.title: Days, months and seasons
body: All days are **masculine** (*der Montag*), all months are **masculine** (*der Mai*), all seasons are **masculine** (*der Sommer*). One gender for the whole calendar — for once German is being kind.
after: *Mittwoch* ("mid-week") is the only day that doesn't end in *-tag*, and that makes sense: the German week starts on **Monday**, so Wednesday really is right in the middle. ⚠️ German calendars put *Montag* in the first column, not *Sonntag* — watch for this when reading schedules.
Saturday has two names: *Samstag* in the south and west (and on official broadcasts), *Sonnabend* in the northeast. Both are correct; *Samstag* is safer for beginners.
The four seasons: *der Frühling* (spring), *der Sommer* (summer), *der Herbst* (fall), *der Winter* (winter). They all take *im*: *im Sommer*, *im Winter*.

grammars.title: Ordinal numbers and dates
body: Ordinals are formed by adding **-te** to the numbers 1-19 and **-ste** from 20 on. Written as a figure, the marker is a **period**: *3. Mai* is read *dritter Mai* (like English *3rd May*).
after: The five odd ones are marked in bold: *erste*, *dritte*, *siebte*, *achte*, and the switch to *-ste* from twenty on. The rest are completely uniform — just as English has its own odd ones in *first*, *second*, *third*.

In a sentence, the form changes slightly depending on its position: ***Heute ist der** dritte Mai* (naming), but ***Ich komme am** dritt**en** Mai* (when something happens). Rule of thumb: after *am*, always **-en**.

Dates are written **day.month.year**: *11.09.2026* means September 11, not November 9. This is the British habit and the reverse of the American one — and misreading it is the most common way to miss an appointment.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Appointments in Germany are taken more seriously than in many other places. Turning up fifteen minutes late without a word is already considered rude, and canceling a doctor's appointment less than 24 hours ahead can be billed. Better learn *Ich muss den Termin absagen* now, not later.

blocks.text: Notice the forms *montags*, *dienstags*, *freitags* — lowercase, ending in -s, and meaning "every such day". *Ich arbeite **montags*** = I work on Mondays, unlike *Ich arbeite **am Montag*** = I'm working this Monday.

Shops in Germany close completely on public holidays and every Sunday — not closing early, but closed. It's the first surprise for almost every newcomer, and it has real consequences: shopping on Saturday isn't an option, it's a must.

blocks.title: Three sentences to learn whole
items: *Welcher Tag ist heute?* — What day is it today?
*Der wievielte ist heute?* — What's the date today?
*Heute ist Donnerstag, der elfte September.* — Today is Thursday, September eleventh.
Am Dienstag habe ich leider Kurs.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
